project_name: King County Library System Administration Module
initial_requirements: King County Library System needs a central administration module for its multi-branch Integrated Library System. System administrators should be able to configure library processes, manage users, groups, and privileges, monitor and troubleshoot servers, databases, applications, services, and interfaces, coordinate software updates, and protect operational data through backup and recovery. The module must support centralized administration without disrupting daily library services.

topics.topic_content: Privilege assignment and access boundaries

slots.value: Privileges should be role-based and limited to people who actually need them for their job, with stronger restrictions on anything that can be changed versus just viewed. Sensitive records like audit logs, account details, and backup information should be visible to administrators and support staff only when they are handling a legitimate operational issue, with write access tightly controlled. If the data includes patron or security-related information, it should be masked or partially displayed unless someone has an approved reason to see the full record. Access for troubleshooting by someone outside the normal admin role should be temporary, logged, and escalated through the appropriate support process. Access should be limited to administrators and support staff who are actively responsible for monitoring or resolving the issue, and only for the systems they need to touch; if a record contains security-sensitive details, it should be even more restricted, with audit logging on every view or change. Records tied to an external interface or a security issue should be treated as highly sensitive by default, with access limited to the smallest support group that can work the issue. If they need to be shared wider for investigation, that should be temporary and deliberate, not the normal state. Administrators should be able to inspect status, review logs, restart services, clear stuck jobs, and verify connectivity or configuration when needed; disabling or re-enabling an interface may be allowed but should be controlled because it can affect branch operations. Anything that changes data or has a broad service impact should be more tightly restricted and probably require additional approval or at least a clear audit trail. Anything that can interrupt branch operations should be limited to authorized administrators with a clear operational need, ideally done during a low-impact window if timing matters, and disabling or re-enabling an interface should have explicit approval or documented authorization. For the most critical operational data, every update should be captured essentially immediately; changes to access, configuration, and recovery-related information cannot afford even a few minutes of data loss, while clearly transient or informational items that do not affect the actual system state may be exempt.

slots.value: Must preserve auditability so the system can show who changed a record and when; administrators need to understand how approvals and audit trails work. For records tied to an external interface or a security issue, every access, export, or change should be logged. Hold placement and hold clearance should also be logged with who approved it and why. In an emergency hold placement, the reason, time, and who took the action must be documented right away, then reviewed afterward by the regular authority. Every audit log entry should at least include the user ID or role that performed the action, the exact timestamp, the action taken, the record or case affected, and the stated reason or ticket number behind it. For changes to the hold itself, the log should also capture the previous state and the new state. For approval-based actions, the approving person or authority should be recorded, plus any reference to the incident, audit, or legal matter that justified it.

Archiving applies when a record is no longer needed for day-to-day operations but still has audit, history, or troubleshooting value, or is rarely accessed but still needed; deletion applies only when the retention period has expired and there is no remaining business, legal, or operational reason to keep it. Open audit, legal hold, incident review, or ongoing troubleshooting cases extend retention beyond the normal threshold, and the record must be locked from deletion until the hold is cleared or the case is closed. Only authorized roles such as system administrators or a designated records/compliance authority can place or clear a hold, and that action should be logged with who approved it and why; clearing a hold should require the same level of authority as placing it or at least a formal approval trail. While deletion is blocked, the record should remain readable for audit or investigation but not editable in a way that breaks the evidence trail; necessary changes should be handled through new versions or append-only history rather than overwriting the retained record.

topics.topic_content: Incident diagnosis and operational troubleshooting

slots.value: Troubleshooting actions that can interrupt branch operations should be limited to authorized administrators with a clear operational need and ideally performed during a low-impact window when timing matters. Disabling or re-enabling an interface should require an explicit approval step or at least documented authorization, should be fully logged for later review, and should be visible to other support staff so they know what was changed and why. If there is any doubt about impact, central operations should sign off before it happens.

slots.value: Audit logs, operational status data from servers, databases, applications, and interfaces, plus reporting and auditing to see who changed what and when; preserve auditability so changes show who changed a record and when. Access should be role-based and limited to people who actually need it for their job, with stronger restrictions on anything that can be changed versus just viewed. Sensitive records like audit logs, account details, and backup information should be visible to administrators and support staff only when they’re handling a legitimate operational issue, and write access should be tightly controlled. If the data includes patron or security-related information, use masking or partial display unless someone has an approved reason to see the full record. Access for troubleshooting by someone outside the normal admin role should be temporary and logged, with escalation through the appropriate support process. Anything that shows system health, error details, or interface activity should be handled more carefully because it can expose a lot about the environment, and those logs and monitoring records should have tighter access than ordinary administrative data, with a clear audit trail of who viewed or changed them.

slots.key: Access control and elevated approval for administrative changes
slots.value: Only authorized staff can make changes; version upgrades definitely need approval and extra review, especially if they touch the core application or database. Security patches are important too, but may move faster if delaying them increases risk. Any update that could affect integrations, interfaces, or service availability should also be treated as high-impact, including dependency changes and configuration changes that come with the update; high-impact status depends on whether the update could interrupt service, noticeably change behavior, or require coordination with branches. A second approver is required for changes that could affect many branches, alter security permissions, interrupt service, or change core circulation or integration settings, especially if the change is hard to roll back or could impact patron service.

slots.key: Retention and privacy constraints for operational data
slots.value: Follow retention and privacy expectations for operational data, especially staff accounts and troubleshooting logs. Keep these records only as long as needed for operations, audits, incident follow-up, legal hold, and recurring troubleshooting, then archive or delete according to county policy and legal requirements. Privacy handling should be stricter for anything that can identify a person or reveal system behavior in a security-sensitive way, with access limited and logged. Longer retention or fuller access is appropriate during an active incident, a compliance hold, a formal investigation that requires the records, or while the records may still be needed for audit, legal hold, recurring troubleshooting, or an open incident review. Anything with legal, audit, incident review, or troubleshooting value should be protected from deletion until formally cleared; if a record is still needed but rarely accessed, archive it, and delete only when the retention period has expired and there is no remaining business, legal, or operational reason to keep it.

slots.key: Data ownership and source of truth
slots.value: The central administration module should stay the source of truth for records that affect security, shared workflows, or system-wide behavior. Branches or other systems may request the change or supply input, but the central module should own the authoritative update so everyone stays consistent. Another system may write directly only when it is clearly the designated owner of that data and there is a controlled integration in place. If ownership is unclear, or if two places could disagree, central control should win.

slots.key: Retention extension for holds and active cases
slots.value: Open audits, legal holds, incident reviews, and ongoing troubleshooting cases should extend retention beyond the normal threshold, and the record should be locked from deletion until the hold or case is formally cleared. While deletion is blocked, the record should remain readable for audit or investigation, but not editable in a way that breaks the evidence trail; any necessary changes should be handled through versioning or append-only history rather than overwriting the retained record. For held records, direct edits should be blocked and only append-only notes or a new version through a controlled update process should be allowed. If absolutely necessary, limited fields such as a status flag or case classification may change, but only under tight control with the old value preserved in history. Attachments tied to the held record should usually not be replaced or deleted unless the system preserves the prior version; attachment changes are allowed only for clear compliance or privacy reasons, such as redacting personal data. The original attachment should be preserved in a protected form, replacement or versioning should keep the new file clearly linked to the old one and retain both versions with full history, and deletion should not be allowed while the hold is active unless legal counsel or a designated records authority approves it and the action is fully documented. Any such change should record who approved it, what was changed, why it was necessary, and keep an immutable trail of the original attachment and all versions.

topics.topic_content: External systems and interface dependencies

slots.value: Multiple systems or branches must be touched separately for access updates and configuration changes; branch-specific workstations or anything that doesn’t connect to shared services can usually be updated locally, but changes touching core ILS, shared databases, authentication, interfaces, or anything affecting more than one branch should be scheduled centrally. If the action only affects one branch’s own local environment, it can stay local as long as it doesn’t impact shared services or other branches. If it touches a shared server, central database, common interface, or anything that could cascade to multiple branches, it should be treated as system-wide and handled centrally. The practical line is whether the change has isolated impact or shared impact.

slots.value: Synchronization timing should depend on how critical the data is and how much delay the library can tolerate. Account or circulation-related updates should run near real-time or frequently, while less urgent data can run on a schedule to reduce load. Sensitive interfaces or busy downstream systems may need delayed or queued sync to avoid overloading shared services. Event-triggered sync is appropriate for specific actions such as patron updates or status changes when the integration can handle it reliably. Changes that directly affect patron service should be prioritized and run as soon as the system can safely handle them; if either system is under heavy load, the change should be queued rather than dropped unless it is truly nonessential, and syncing should be slowed when needed to avoid overwhelming downstream systems.

slots.value: Retention periods depend on county policy and legal requirements and need verification with the team. Change history and status records should be kept long enough to support audits, troubleshooting, and accountability, with the record preserving who made the change, when it happened, what was changed, and ideally the before-and-after values for important settings. The detail should be preserved as long as the record is kept. For operational logs, enough history should be kept to investigate incidents without overloading the system with unnecessary old data. Different kinds of records should have different retention periods; security-related changes, privilege changes, and anything tied to incidents or compliance should be kept longer than routine status data. Records should be kept as long as they may still be needed for audit, legal hold, or recurring troubleshooting, and only archived or deleted after that window closes. Anything with legal or incident value should be protected from deletion until it is formally cleared. Open audit, legal hold, incident review, or ongoing troubleshooting cases should extend retention beyond the normal threshold, and the record should be locked from deletion until the hold is cleared or the case is closed. When a hold is cleared, it should follow the same level of authority as placing it or at least a formal approval trail.

slots.key: Retention and privacy constraints for operational data
slots.value: Follow retention and privacy expectations for operational data, especially staff accounts and troubleshooting logs. Staff account records should be kept only as long as they’re needed for active employment, audit, or security purposes. Troubleshooting logs should also be time-limited and have tighter access because they can contain sensitive system details or user-related information. Data should be deleted or purged according to policy rather than kept indefinitely. Access should be limited to administrators who need it for their job, and anything tied to audits, security incidents, or unresolved operational problems may be retained longer but only with stricter access controls. Logs and monitoring records that show system health, error details, or interface activity should be treated more carefully and may require shorter retention for routine diagnostics but longer retention for incident investigation or compliance needs.

slots.value: Synchronization frequency should depend on how critical the data is and how much delay the library can tolerate. Account or circulation-related updates should sync near real-time or frequently, while less urgent data can run on a schedule to reduce load. If an interface is sensitive or the downstream system is busy, sync may need to be delayed or queued to avoid overloading shared services. Event-triggered sync is appropriate when a specific action occurs, such as a patron update or status change, as long as the integration can handle it reliably. Changes that directly affect patron service should be prioritized and run as soon as the system can safely handle them; if either system is under heavy load, queue the change rather than drop it unless it is truly nonessential. When there is a risk of overwhelming a downstream system, slow the sync rather than forcing it through, to protect service continuity and stability.

topics.topic_content: Software update coordination across the ILS environment

slots.value: Coordinate software updates centrally across all branches so changes can be applied consistently while normal library service continues. If a change only affects one branch's own staff, workflow, or local settings and does not touch shared services, it can proceed independently. If it affects shared services that other branches rely on, such as a shared catalog rule, circulation policy, user privilege, or an interface, it needs coordination or a wider change. Updates limited to a branch-specific workstation or something that doesn’t connect to shared services can usually be applied locally. If an update touches the core ILS, shared databases, authentication, interfaces, or anything that could affect more than one branch, it should be scheduled centrally so timing and rollback are controlled. If the issue is clearly cross-branch or tied to a shared service, central should take ownership right away because one branch can’t really coordinate that on its own. If it’s local but has ripple effects, the branch can lead initially, but central should be pulled in quickly to coordinate and avoid conflicting actions. The practical rule is whoever has the best visibility and authority over the impacted service should own the response, while the other side stays informed and supports. If response speed matters, there should be a quick handoff path so ownership doesn’t get stuck in debate. If the action only affects one branch’s local environment, it can stay local as long as it doesn’t impact shared services or other branches. If it touches a shared server, central database, common interface, or anything that could cascade to multiple branches, then it should be treated as system-wide and handled centrally. The practical line is whether the change has isolated impact or shared impact. If there’s any real chance it could affect more than one branch, central review or control is required before it goes ahead. A branch can keep ownership if the issue is clearly rooted in something local and the other-branch impact is only indirect or not yet confirmed; once there’s credible evidence that a shared service, central database, or interface is involved, central ownership should take over. Branch staff remain part of the response, but the central team should lead anything that can spread beyond one branch to keep the response coordinated and avoid conflicting changes.
